presentingComplaint: High-grade continuous fever for 10 days with abdominal discomfort, headache and worsening lethargy despite two prior courses of oral antibiotics.
history: Previously well university student from Karachi visiting family in Delhi, presents with a 10-day history of insidious-onset fever that has climbed in a stepwise fashion to 39.5-40 C, now sustained rather than intermittent. He describes frontal headache, marked anorexia, dull peri-umbilical/right-lower-quadrant abdominal discomfort and abdominal fullness, with alternating loose stools and constipation. He drank untreated water and ate street food shortly before onset. His GP started oral ciprofloxacin on day 3 with no defervescence, then switched to oral cefixime on day 7, again without response - hence the concern for a drug-resistant organism. No respiratory symptoms, dysuria, jaundice or rash noted by the patient. No prior typhoid vaccination. No known TB contact. This is a resistant/MDR-organism scenario: failure of both fluoroquinolone and oral third-generation cephalosporin points to fluoroquinolone-non-susceptible and possibly XDR Salmonella Typhi originating from the endemic Indus-valley clone, requiring in-patient escalation and search for a suppurative complication (source control).
examination: Ill and apathetic but oriented, flushed. Coated tongue. A few blanching, 2-3 mm pink macules (rose spots) noted on the lower chest and upper abdomen. Abdomen soft with mild diffuse tenderness and a palpable, non-tender liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin and a just-palpable spleen tip. No peritonism, no guarding, bowel sounds present. Chest clear, no murmur. No focal neurology, no neck stiffness. No peripheral oedema.

labs.note: Leukopenia with relative eosinopenia, mild thrombocytopenia and modest transaminitis - typical of enteric fever; anaemia mild.

imaging: Ultrasound abdomen: mild hepatosplenomegaly with prominent mesenteric lymph nodes and a trace of pelvic free fluid; no liver abscess, no gallbladder or biliary pathology, no bowel-wall thickening to suggest perforation. Erect chest/abdominal film: no free air.
microbiology: Blood cultures (two sets, drawn before escalation) grew Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi. Susceptibility: RESISTANT to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, co-trimoxazole (classic MDR), ciprofloxacin (MIC high; also nalidixic-acid resistant) AND ceftriaxone/cefixime (blaCTX-M-15 ESBL) - i.e. an extensively drug-resistant (XDR) S. Typhi. SUSCEPTIBLE to azithromycin and meropenem. Stool culture pending. Widal single high titre is supportive but non-diagnostic and not relied upon.
finalDiagnosis: Enteric (typhoid) fever due to extensively drug-resistant (XDR) Salmonella Typhi
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e - Enteric (Typhoid) Fever
stewardship: Blood-culture-confirmed XDR S. Typhi that has clinically failed both a fluoroquinolone and an oral third-generation cephalosporin. Empiric guideline-concordant therapy for suspected enteric fever in a South-Asian traveller with prior treatment failure should already cover resistant strains: IV ceftriaxone is standard first-line empiric cover, but in this high-XDR-prevalence setting with documented cephalosporin failure, ESCALATE to IV meropenem (or high-dose azithromycin for non-severe disease). De-escalate/narrow once susceptibilities confirm - here oral/IV azithromycin can complete therapy as the organism is azithromycin-susceptible and the patient is not severely ill. Total duration 10-14 days. 'Source control' in enteric fever means active exclusion and management of suppurative/perforative complications (intestinal perforation, GI bleed, cholecystitis with chronic carriage) - none present here, so no surgical intervention required. Public-health notification and safe-water/food counselling; screen for chronic biliary carriage if fever relapses.
contraindications: Avoid continued fluoroquinolone or oral 3rd-gen cephalosporin monotherapy given documented resistance and clinical failure
Avoid empiric oral cefixime for confirmed/suspected XDR strains
Caution with carbapenems if documented beta-lactam anaphylaxis
edgeCases: Intestinal perforation or GI haemorrhage in the 3rd week - watch for sudden abdominal pain, peritonism or melena mandating surgical source control
Relapse after apparent cure suggests inadequate duration or chronic biliary carriage
Co-endemic malaria/dengue may coexist - smear and NS1/serology if course atypical

Typhi in a South-Asian traveller = enteric fever; failure of fluoroquinolone and oral cephalosporin signals XDR requiring escalation to meropenem/azithromycin.
